opus-5.5.text:
I think it's because both sides are moving at the same time, and most of the difficulty lives in the gap between them.

If you only think about methods, it's actually not that hard to come up with something. You can make a model bigger, add a new training trick, design a prompting scheme. People are very good at that, and the whole field has been trained for years to think that way: here's a fixed benchmark, beat the number. Similarly, if you only think about tasks, you can imagine a lot of things you'd like AI to do. Book a flight, write software, do science. That's easy to dream about too.

The hard part is finding a task where a method actually *works* and where that working *means something*. If the task is too easy, the method looks good but you learn nothing. If the task is too far away, nothing works and you also learn nothing. You need a task that's just at the edge, where a new idea can make it go from "basically impossible" to "kind of possible," and where that change tells you something general about intelligence, not just about that benchmark.

When I was working on language agents, things like ReAct or the web shopping environment, a lot of the time wasn't spent on the method itself. The method, honestly, is often simple. The time went into asking: what's the right environment, what's the right interface, what's the right way to measure success, so that reasoning and acting together actually matter? If you set up the task badly, a very simple baseline beats you, or the result doesn't transfer to anything real.

And there's another layer. Methods are getting more and more general. Once you have a strong pretrained model, plus reasoning, plus RL, a lot of methods that used to be task-specific stop mattering, because the general recipe just works across many tasks. So the bottleneck moves. It's less "can I invent a clever method" and more "can I define a task that's both valuable and that pushes the general recipe in a new direction." That's the shift I think of as the second half of AI: evaluation and problem definition become as important as, maybe more important than, the training method.

So to me, the fit is hardest because it requires taste on both sides at once. You need to understand what current methods can almost do, and you need to understand what problems in the real world are worth solving, and then find the small intersection where those overlap. That intersection is small, it moves every few months, and nobody hands it to you.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's because most of the time in research, you have one thing but not the other. Either you have a method you're really excited about and you're searching for a problem where it actually matters, or you have a task that clearly matters and you have no idea what tool would crack it. And people usually underestimate how rare it is for the two to line up.

Take my own experience. When I worked on Tree of Thoughts, the idea of doing search over reasoning steps wasn't new at all. Search is one of the oldest ideas in AI. The hard part wasn't the method, it was finding a task like Game of 24 or creative writing where chain of thought clearly fails in a way that search clearly fixes. If you pick a task that's too easy, the method looks unnecessary. If you pick one that's too hard, nothing works and you learn nothing. You need the task to sit in exactly the right band of difficulty.

Same with ReAct. Combining reasoning and acting sounds obvious in hindsight. But if I had tested it on a benchmark where you just need to call one API, nobody would have cared. It only became interesting on tasks like HotpotQA or ALFWorld, where you actually need to think about what you've seen before deciding what to do next. The task revealed the method.

And I think this is also why the taste of a researcher is so hard to teach. Reading papers gives you a library of methods. Running experiments gives you a sense of tasks. But knowing that this particular method and this particular task belong together, before you've run anything, that's almost an intuition. It comes from having failed many times at mismatches. I've spent months on methods that were elegant and tasks that were important, and the combination was just dead, because the task didn't have the structure the method was exploiting.

So I'd say the method is maybe twenty percent of the work and the task is twenty percent, and the remaining sixty is the fit. That's where the actual research judgment lives.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest part is that the method and the task are both moving targets. If you start with a method you like, it’s easy to look for a task where it produces a better number. But that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve solved an important problem. And if you start with a very ambitious task, you may not have a way to make progress or even measure whether your idea is working.

So you need to move between the two. What is actually preventing us from solving this task? Does the method address that bottleneck? And can you design an experiment that tells you whether your intuition is right, rather than just whether the final score went up?

Once that fit is clear, the research becomes much more concrete. You can implement something, test it, and iterate. Before that, you’re dealing with uncertainty about the question itself. You might spend a lot of time doing technically good work and only later realize that the method wasn’t addressing what mattered. That’s why I see finding the fit as the hardest part—it requires judgment about both what is worth solving and what you can meaningfully contribute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hard because neither side is fixed. You don’t start with a perfectly defined task and then simply choose the best method. Often, you have an intuition about a method, and you’re trying to understand what problem it actually solves. Or you have a problem you care about, but the methods available don’t quite address the part that matters.

Once you find that fit, the work becomes much clearer: you can implement the idea, run experiments, and improve it. Before that, a disappointing result is ambiguous. Is the method wrong? Is the task unsuitable? Is the implementation bad? Or are you measuring the wrong thing? You have to make progress without being able to separate those explanations cleanly.

So for me, research is an iterative process of refining both the method and the question. The difficult part is finding a pairing where the method addresses a real bottleneck, and the task makes its value visible. That takes more judgment than simply making a model perform better on a fixed benchmark.
